---
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:separate}
If $F$ is concave in each coordinate separately, then
\[
 F(x)\ge\sum_{S\subseteq N}F(\mathbf 1_S)\prod_{i\in S}x_i\prod_{i\notin S}(1-x_i).
\]
Consequently, a Boolean-nonnegative DR-submodular polynomial is nonnegative throughout the cube.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For one coordinate, with the others fixed, concavity gives
$F(x)\ge x_iF(x_{-i},1)+(1-x_i)F(x_{-i},0)$. Apply this inequality successively to all coordinates.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:self_atom}
Let $F(t)=t(1-t)$. Its Boolean restriction and the multilinear extension of that restriction are identically zero. Its standard rooted roof is $L(t)=\min\{t,1-t\}$, while $F(1/2)=1/4$. The \emph{continuous concave envelope}, the smallest concave majorant on the interval, is $F$ itself because $F$ is concave. Thus the Boolean concave closure, the continuous concave envelope, and the standard roof are three different functions. In particular, a Boolean closure need not majorize a continuous objective.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:common}
Let $\mathcal K\subseteq[0,1]^N$ be nonempty, compact, and down-closed, let $F$ be continuous, and let $H$ be real-valued and upper semicontinuous on $\mathcal K$. Suppose
\[
 \max_{\mathcal K}H\ge\max_{\mathcal K}F.
\]
Let $k\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_k$ be downward maps, and let $p_s\ge0$ sum to one, and let $\rho\ge0$. If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:common_inequality}
 \sum_s p_sF(R_s(x))\ge\rho H(x)\qquad(x\in\mathcal K),
\end{equation}
then, for every $\delta\ge0$, a feasible $\bar x$ satisfying $H(\bar x)\ge\max_\mathcal K H-\delta$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:common_guarantee}
 \max_sF(R_s(\bar x))\ge\rho\max_{x\in\mathcal K}F(x)-\rho\delta.
\end{equation}
Every recovered point is feasible.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Down-closedness gives feasibility. The largest branch value dominates the weighted average, which is at least $\rho H(\bar x)\ge\rho(\max_\mathcal K H-\delta)\ge\rho(\max_\mathcal K F-\delta)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:aggregation}
Suppose the sums $F=\sum_bw_bF_b$ and $L=\sum_bw_bL_b$ are finite, $w_b\ge0$, and $\rho\ge0$. An active component is one with $w_b>0$. If one fixed probability distribution over downward maps satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:component_payment}
 \sum_sp_sF_b(R_s(x))\ge\rho L_b(x)\qquad\text{for every active component }b,
\end{equation}
then $\sum_sp_sF(R_s(x))\ge\rho L(x)$. If $L\ge F$ and the continuity, compactness, and down-closedness hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:common} hold, that theorem gives its approximation guarantee to \eqref{eq:continuous_problem}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Multiply the component inequalities by $w_b$ and sum. Nonnegative weights preserve their direction, and the same global map in each summand makes the left sides add to $F(R_s(x))$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:quadratic}
Every Boolean-nonnegative quadratic DR polynomial \eqref{eq:quadratic} admits a deterministic $1/2$ approximation over $\mathcal K$, up to any prescribed additive error, under Section~\ref{sec:access}. The same factor applies to every supplied degree-two compatible rooted certificate with its standard roof.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $L_M$ be the standard roof of the certificate for $M$ in \eqref{eq:diagonal_split}. Optimize the hybrid concave roof
\[
 H_F(x)=L_M(x)+\sum_id_ix_i(1-x_i)
\]
to additive accuracy $\delta$, and put $y_i=\phi_2(\bar x_i)$. Equation~\eqref{eq:clipping} pays each rooted quadratic term and positive unary by $1/2$; constants and complemented unaries lose no value. Clipping also preserves the diagonal residual: if $\bar x_i\le1/2$, then $y_i=\bar x_i$; otherwise
\[
 y_i(1-y_i)-\bar x_i(1-\bar x_i)
 =\tfrac14-\bar x_i(1-\bar x_i)=(\bar x_i-1/2)^2\ge0.
\]
Consequently $F(y)\ge H_F(\bar x)/2\ge\operatorname{OPT}(F,\mathcal K)/2-\delta/2$. Choose tolerances with total loss at most $\varepsilon$. For a supplied degree-two compatible certificate, the positive and complemented uniform-polarity atoms satisfy the same clipping inequality. A mixed atom has the form $(1-a)(1-u)$, including identified coordinates, and roof $\min\{1-a,1-u\}$. Both recovered factors are at least $1/2$ and dominate their original values, so their product is at least half this roof. Constants and complemented unaries lose no value, so aggregation gives the same factor for its standard roof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:quadratic_box}
Let $B=\prod_i[\alpha_i,\beta_i]$ be a nonempty finite box with rational bounds, and let $F$ be a lattice-submodular quadratic with rational coefficients, nonnegative on $B$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns $z\in B$ with
\[
 F(z)\ge\tfrac12\max_{x\in B}F(x)-\varepsilon.
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Substitute fixed coordinates and map each remaining interval to $[0,1]$ by $x_i=\alpha_i+(\beta_i-\alpha_i)t_i$. If none remain, return the unique point. This positive affine change preserves degree, mixed derivative signs, and nonnegativity. Work with the normalized polynomial and its surrogate \eqref{eq:quadratic_chord}.

Starting from any $y$ in the normalized cube, visit the coordinates in $I_+$ once. Replace the current coordinate by whichever endpoint, zero or one, gives the larger value of $G$, choosing zero in a tie. Affinity in that coordinate means the replacement cannot decrease $G$. At the final point $z$, every correction in \eqref{eq:quadratic_chord} vanishes, so $F(z)=G(z)\ge G(y)$. Applying this procedure to a maximizer of $G$, and using $G\ge F$, proves
\[
 \max_{[0,1]^n}G=\max_{[0,1]^n}F.
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:quadratic} gives a rational point $y$ with $G(y)\ge\tfrac12\max G-\varepsilon$. The endpoint procedure transfers this guarantee to $F$ without further loss. Map its output back to $B$. Normalization and its inverse have polynomial encoding length; the added step uses at most $2|I_+|$ exact rational value evaluations.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:quadratic_box}
On $[0,1]^2$, take
\[
 F(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+(1-x_1)x_2+x_2(1-x_2).
\]
This function is nonnegative and lattice submodular, while $\partial_{11}^2F=2>0$. Replacing $x_1^2$ by $x_1$ gives $G=x_1(1-x_2)+x_2+x_2(1-x_2)$, with hybrid roof
\[
 H_G(x)=\min\{x_1,1-x_2\}+x_2+x_2(1-x_2)
       \le1+x_2-x_2^2\le5/4.
\]
The point $\bar x=(1/2,1/2)$ attains this roof bound. Clipping leaves it fixed, with $G(\bar x)=1$ and $F(\bar x)=3/4$. Comparing $G(0,1/2)=3/4$ and $G(1,1/2)=5/4$ chooses $z=(1,1/2)$. Thus $F(z)=5/4$, attaining the certified optimum while retaining a fractional coordinate with negative curvature.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{hard:prop:cut-equivalence}
A quadratic submodular pseudo-Boolean function is globally nonnegative if
and only if it is the cut-value function of a directed graph with
nonnegative arc weights and two fixed terminals.  A representation can be
constructed in polynomial time, and the cardinality of $S$ equals the number
of selected nonterminal vertices.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The orientation construction in Section~\ref{sec:quadratic_orientation} gives the nonnegative coefficients in \eqref{hard:eq:cut-decomposition}, with $r=\min_S f(S)$. Introduce arcs $s\to t$, $i\to t$, $s\to i$, and $i\to j$ with weights $r,p_i,q_i$, and $\theta_{ij}$, respectively. The cut leaving $\{s\}\cup S$ has value $M(\mathbf 1_S)=f(S)$. Its number of selected nonterminal vertices is exactly $|S|$, so the original cardinality budget is preserved. The orientation program and the graph construction have polynomial encoding length.

Conversely, a fixed-terminal directed cut with nonnegative arc weights is a nonnegative sum of $1$, $x_i$, $1-x_i$, and $x_i(1-x_j)$ after zero-contribution arcs are discarded. Its value function is globally nonnegative, quadratic, and submodular.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:cubic_DR}
The polynomial \eqref{eq:cubic_input} is DR-submodular on the cube if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic_DR}
 q_\alpha+\sum_{\substack{|\beta|=3\\\beta\ge\alpha}}
 \binom\beta\alpha[t_\beta]_+\le0\qquad(|\alpha|=2).
\end{equation}
This includes $\alpha=2e_i$, hence the diagonal conditions.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $|\alpha|=2$, the normalized second derivative is the affine function
\[
 \frac1{\alpha!}\partial^\alpha F(x)
 =q_\alpha+\sum_{\substack{|\beta|=3\\\beta\ge\alpha}}
   \binom\beta\alpha t_\beta x^{\beta-\alpha}.
\]
Its cube maximum sets to one exactly those coordinates with positive coefficients. The resulting maximum is the left side of \eqref{eq:cubic_DR}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:orientation}
The value of \eqref{eq:orientation} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orientation_value}
 c-\sum_{\beta\in H^-}d_\beta-\min_{S\subseteq N}F(\mathbf 1_S).
\end{equation}
If $F$ is Boolean-nonnegative, an optimal solution yields a nonnegative uniform-polarity rooted certificate of the same maximum literal degree, with residual constant exactly $\min_SF(\mathbf 1_S)$. The certificate is computable by a rational linear program of size polynomial in the sparse support-incidence input. Conversely, a nonnegative certificate implies nonnegativity on the cube.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
An arbitrary distribution of each coefficient becomes feasible after increasing $q_i$ sufficiently. Eliminating the dual variables for the equality constraints gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orientation_dual}
 \max_{0\le u\le1}\left\{
 \sum_\eta b_\eta\min_{i\in\operatorname{supp}\eta}u_i
 -\sum_\beta d_\beta\max_{i\in\operatorname{supp}\beta}u_i-\sum_i a_iu_i\right\}.
\end{equation}
For $S_t=\{i:u_i\ge t\}$, integrate the identities
\[
 u_i=\int_0^1\mathbf 1\{i\in S_t\}\,dt,\quad
 \min_{i\in T}u_i=\int_0^1\mathbf 1\{T\subseteq S_t\}\,dt,\quad
 \max_{i\in T}u_i=\int_0^1\mathbf 1\{T\cap S_t\ne\varnothing\}\,dt.
\]
The dual objective becomes
\[
 \int_0^1\left[
 \sum_{\eta:\operatorname{supp}\eta\subseteq S_t}b_\eta
 -\sum_{\beta:\operatorname{supp}\beta\cap S_t\ne\varnothing}d_\beta
 -\sum_{i\in S_t}a_i\right]dt.
\]
This average cannot exceed the largest bracketed set value, and the corresponding Boolean vector attains that value. At a set $S$, the bracket equals $c-\sum_\beta d_\beta-F(\mathbf 1_S)$. Strong linear-programming duality gives \eqref{eq:orientation_value}.

Set
\[
 p_i=a_i-\sum_\eta\theta^+_{\eta,i}+\sum_\beta\theta^-_{\beta,i}+q_i,
 \qquad c_0=c-\sum_\beta d_\beta-\sum_iq_i.
\]
Missing root-index terms are zero. The constraints give $p_i\ge0$, and the optimum value gives $c_0=\min_SF(\mathbf 1_S)\ge0$. Expanding
\begin{align*}
 F(x)={}&c_0+\sum_ip_ix_i+\sum_iq_i(1-x_i)\\
 &+\sum_{\eta,i}\theta^+_{\eta,i}(x_i-x^\eta)
 +\sum_{\beta,i}\theta^-_{\beta,i}\bigl((1-x_i)-(1-x)^\beta\bigr)
\end{align*}
recovers every coefficient of \eqref{eq:uniform_negaform}. Each atom is nonnegative because its root is one of the factors in the product. All operations have polynomial encoding length.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:cubic_certificate}
Every Boolean-nonnegative cubic DR polynomial has a polynomially constructible nonnegative uniform-polarity rooted certificate of literal degree at most three. Its optimally oriented residual constant is its minimum Boolean value. Conversely, every nonnegative sum of constants, literals, and uniform-polarity rooted atoms of literal degree at most three is Boolean-nonnegative and DR-submodular.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For each positive cubic coefficient, use the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic_complement}
 x^\beta=1-\sum_i\beta_ix_i+
 \sum_{\substack{|\alpha|=2\\\alpha\le\beta}}\binom\beta\alpha x^\alpha
 -(1-x)^\beta\qquad(|\beta|=3).
\end{equation}
The remaining quadratic coefficients are nonpositive by Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic_DR}. The result is a uniform-polarity negaform of literal degree at most three. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:orientation}. Conversely, each uniform-polarity atom has nonpositive diagonal and mixed second partials: its nonlinear part is the negative of a product of literals of one polarity. Nonnegative sums preserve this property and nonnegativity.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:cubic_maps}
For $m=1,2$, $\sigma\in\{+,-\}$, and all occurrence-slot values,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic_slot_inequalities}
 8h_m^\sigma(\phi_0(a),\phi_0(u))+
 9h_m^\sigma(\phi_1(a),\phi_1(u))\ge8\ell_m^\sigma(a,u).
\end{equation}
Also $8\phi_0(t)+9\phi_1(t)\ge8t$ for $t\in[0,1]$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{app:cubic} proves the inequalities by checking the breakpoints and certifying the switching faces. The slots range independently over real values, so the same inequalities hold when repeated occurrences are identified.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:cubic}
Under Section~\ref{sec:access}, every explicitly represented Boolean-nonnegative cubic DR polynomial admits a deterministic $8/17$ approximation over $\mathcal K$, up to any prescribed additive error. More generally, the same elementary portfolio applies to any supplied certificate in $\mathfrak C_{\le3}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:cubic_certificate} constructs a uniform-polarity certificate for the intrinsic polynomial class. Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic_maps} pays its atoms and positive unaries, while constants and complemented unaries lose no value. Add these common inequalities using Corollary~\ref{cor:aggregation}. For supplied compatible certificates, Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed} covers the mixed-polarity atoms. If $\bar x$ is a $\delta$-accurate roof optimizer, Theorem~\ref{thm:common} gives value at least $8(\operatorname{OPT}(F,\mathcal K)-\delta)/17$ for the better of $\phi_0(\bar x)$ and $\phi_1(\bar x)$. Allocate the numerical errors as in Section~\ref{sec:access}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:certificate}
An exact negaform is a polynomial identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:negaform}
 F(x)=A(x)-\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}b_\sigma m_\sigma(x),\qquad b_\sigma\ge0,
\end{equation}
where $A$ is affine. For any occurrence index $r\in\{1,\ldots,d_\sigma\}$ in $m_\sigma$, rooting at $r$ defines two functions:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:atom_roof}
 h_{\sigma,r}=\lambda_{\sigma r}-m_\sigma,
 \qquad
 \ell_{\sigma,r}=\min\left\{\lambda_{\sigma r},\sum_{q\ne r}(1-\lambda_{\sigma q})\right\}.
\end{equation}
The distinguished occurrence is the \emph{root}; the remaining occurrences are its \emph{heads}. An expression $h_{\sigma,r}$ is a \emph{rooted atom}. A root is \emph{polarity-compatible} if a positive-only monomial uses a positive root and every monomial containing a complemented occurrence uses a complemented root. A nonnegative compatible rooted certificate subordinate to \eqref{eq:negaform} is an identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:root_certificate}
 F(x)=c_0+\sum_i p_ix_i+\sum_i q_i(1-x_i)
       +\sum_{\sigma,r}\theta_{\sigma,r}h_{\sigma,r}(x),
\end{equation}
with all coefficients nonnegative, all selected roots compatible, and
$\sum_r\theta_{\sigma,r}=b_\sigma$. Let $\mathfrak C_{\le d}$ denote the cone generated by the constant function one, literals, and compatible rooted atoms of literal degree at most $d$. Here a \emph{conic combination} is a finite sum with nonnegative coefficients, and the cone generated by a family consists of all its conic combinations.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:root_independence}
For every root occurrence,
\[
 \ell_{\sigma,r}-\lambda_{\sigma r}
 =\min\left\{0,\sum_{q=1}^{d_\sigma}(1-\lambda_{\sigma q})-1\right\}
 =:\psi_\sigma.
\]
Thus a fixed negaform induces the root-independent \emph{standard concave roof}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:standard_roof}
 L_{\mathcal N}(x)=A(x)+\sum_\sigma b_\sigma\psi_\sigma(x).
\end{equation}
It majorizes $F$ on the cube and agrees with $F$ at Boolean points. If a subordinate certificate exists, this is also the sum of its atom roofs and affine terms.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Subtract the root literal from the minimum in \eqref{eq:atom_roof}. The union bound gives
$\lambda_r(1-\prod_{q\ne r}\lambda_q)\le\min\{\lambda_r,\sum_{q\ne r}(1-\lambda_q)\}$.
Each correction $\psi_\sigma$ is concave, since it is the minimum of two affine functions, and the bound is exact for Boolean literal values. Summation and coefficient matching prove the result.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:mixed}
Suppose a downward scalar portfolio pays positive unaries and both slot-atom types through rank $d-1$ by factor $\rho\in[0,1]$. It then pays every compatible rooted certificate in $\mathfrak C_{\le d}$ by the same factor.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
It remains to treat mixed-polarity atoms. Compatibility forces their root to be $1-a$. Write each head literal as $1-v_j$. A complemented head recovers as $1-\phi_s(v_j)$. For a positive head, downwardness gives
\[
 \phi_s(1-v_j)\le1-v_j\le1-\phi_s(v_j).
\]
The recovered head product is therefore no larger than the complemented-only product, and the recovered atom is at least $h_m^-(\phi_s(a),\phi_s(v))$. The roof equals $\ell_m^-(a,v)$. Sum the atom and unary inequalities using Corollary~\ref{cor:aggregation}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:single}
The continuous map \eqref{eq:single_map} satisfies $\gamma_*t\le\phi_*(t)\le t$ and, for every finite $m\ge1$,
\[
 h_m^\sigma(\phi_*(a),\phi_*(u))\ge\gamma_*\ell_m^\sigma(a,u)
 \qquad(\sigma\in\{+,-\}).
\]
No downward scalar map gives a larger common factor for these atoms and positive unaries. No continuity, monotonicity, or measurability is required of a competing map. The upper bound already holds for positive-root atoms of literal degree at most three.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{app:single} proves the inequalities for every finite rank. The matching upper bound in Section~\ref{sec:single_upper} uses only positive-root atoms through rank two and applies to every downward scalar map.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:twelve_atoms}
For $m=1,\ldots,11$, $\sigma\in\{+,-\}$, and $a,u_1,\ldots,u_m\in~[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:twelve}
 8h_m^\sigma(\alpha_{12}(a),\alpha_{12}(u))+
 9h_m^\sigma(\beta_{12}(a),\beta_{12}(u))\ge8\ell_m^\sigma(a,u).
\end{equation}
Moreover $8\alpha_{12}(t)+9\beta_{12}(t)\ge8t$. Repeated variables and literal occurrences are permitted.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{app:twelve} identifies the formal statement and source version proving nonnegativity of both slotwise deficits and the unary deficit. The knot-agreement results match the formal maps to Table~\ref{tab:knots}, and the atom definitions give exactly \eqref{eq:twelve}. Since the inequality holds for all independent slots, identifying slots covers repeated occurrences.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:twelve}
A polynomial supplied with a polynomial-size compatible certificate in $\mathfrak C_{\le12}$ admits a deterministic $8/17$ approximation over $\mathcal K$, up to any prescribed additive error. Optimize its standard roof, apply $\alpha_{12}$ and $\beta_{12}$, and keep the better branch.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:twelve_atoms}, Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:common} with probabilities $8/17,9/17$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:classes}
For $d\ge2$,
\[
 \mathcal R_d\subseteq\mathcal C_d\subseteq\mathcal Q_d,\qquad \mathcal A_d\subseteq\mathcal C_d,
 \qquad \mathcal R_2=\mathcal C_2=\mathcal Q_2,\quad \mathcal R_3=\mathcal C_3=\mathcal Q_3.
\]
On a four-element ground set, $\mathcal R_\infty=\mathcal R_4\subsetneq\mathcal C_4=\mathcal Q_4$. On ground sets of size at least five, $\mathcal C_4$ and $\mathcal R_\infty$ are incomparable. For $d<n$, $\mathcal A_\infty\nsubseteq\mathcal C_d$; for $n\ge4$, $\mathcal A_\infty$ and $\mathcal R_\infty$ are incomparable.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Every rooted function is nonnegative and submodular, and its degree is at most its arity. Nonnegative sums preserve both properties. The decreasing consecutive differences make concave-cardinality functions submodular. The reverse low-degree inclusions follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:orientation} and Proposition~\ref{prop:cubic_certificate}, restricted to multilinear inputs.

On four elements, consider the cardinality sequence $(0,2,3,3,3)$, with polynomial
\[
 F(x)=2\sum_i x_i-\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j+x_1x_2x_3x_4.
\]
Concavity places this function in $\mathcal A_4\subseteq\mathcal C_4$. In a nonnegative uniform-polarity rooted representation, every degree-four monomial has a nonpositive coefficient: a positive rooted product contributes a negative coefficient on its support, and a complemented rooted product contributes a nonpositive coefficient on every four-subset of its support. The positive quartic coefficient therefore excludes $\mathcal R_\infty$, even after embedding the function into a larger ground set. Conversely, $u_{T,i}$ with $|T|=5$ has degree five and cannot belong to $\mathcal C_4$.

The function $S\mapsto\min\{1,|S\cap A|\}$ with $|A|=d+1$ belongs to $\mathcal A_{d+1}$ and has degree $d+1$, excluding $\mathcal C_d$. Finally, $\mathbf 1\{1\in S,2\notin S\}$ cannot be a nonnegative sum of concave-cardinality functions. Restrict any proposed sum to $\{1,2\}$. Because the function vanishes at $\varnothing,\{2\},\{1,2\}$, every nonnegative summand must vanish at these sets. A two-coordinate summand has equal values on the two singletons, and a one-coordinate summand takes its selected value also on $\{1,2\}$. Every summand must consequently vanish at $\{1\}$, a contradiction. The four-element example proves the reverse noninclusion.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:membership}
For each fixed $d$, membership of a rational degree-at-most-$d$ multilinear polynomial in $\mathcal C_d$ is decidable by a rational linear program of size $n^{O(d)}$. A feasible solution supplies a local conic combination.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For each $A\subseteq N$ with $|A|\le d$, enumerate the primitive generators of the cone of nonnegative submodular value tables on $A$. Embed their multilinear coefficient vectors into $N$ and match the input coefficients using nonnegative multipliers. For fixed $d$, the number of generators per support is a constant, and there are $O(n^d)$ supports. The system is feasible precisely when the required decomposition exists.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:arity_four}
Let $g:2^A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ be submodular with $|A|\le4$, and let $G$ be its multilinear extension. For every $x\in[0,1]^A$,
\begin{align}
 G(\phi_*(x))&\ge\gamma_*g^+(x),\label{eq:arity_single}\\
 8G(\psi_0(x))+9G(\psi_1(x))&\ge8g^+(x).\label{eq:arity_pair}
\end{align}
The factor in \eqref{eq:arity_single} is optimal among all downward scalar maps applied commonly to the coordinates, without regularity assumptions. The pair in \eqref{eq:arity_pair} is compatible with arbitrary overlap among local ground sets.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{app:arity_four} describes the finite reduction and the scope of the exact-arithmetic certificates for both inequalities. On four elements the cone has 222 primitive integer rays in 21 permutation orbits. The ray inequalities extend to every $g=\sum_r\lambda_r r$, because
\[
 G=\sum_r\lambda_rG_r,\qquad g^+\le\sum_r\lambda_r r^+,
 \qquad\lambda_r\ge0.
\]
Every ray and local function uses the same maps and weights. Corollary~\ref{cor:aggregation} therefore covers overlapping supports. For fixed-map sharpness in \eqref{eq:arity_single}, use a directed cut on two elements at $x=(1/2,1/2)$. With $z=\phi_*(1/2)=(1+\gamma_*)/4$, its ratio to the closure is $2z(1-z)=\gamma_*$. For optimality among all common downward scalar maps, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:single}: its positive-root witnesses have distinct coordinates and arity at most three, so their roofs are exact closures by \eqref{eq:rooted_closures}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:arity_four}
Given a nonnegative local conic combination of nonnegative submodular functions of arity at most four, optimize \eqref{eq:local_LP}, apply $\psi_0,\psi_1$, and keep the better point. The result is an $8/17$ approximation to the multilinear maximum over $\mathcal K$, up to any prescribed additive error under Section~\ref{sec:access}.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Sum \eqref{eq:arity_pair} and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:common}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:mixed_families}
Suppose a continuous objective is a nonnegative sum of components, each supplied either with a compatible rooted certificate of arbitrary finite literal degree or as the multilinear extension of a nonnegative submodular local function of arity at most four. The sum of the corresponding roofs admits the common recovery factor $\gamma_*$ under $\phi_*$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Theorems~\ref{thm:single} and~\ref{thm:arity_four} use exactly the same scalar map. Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:aggregation}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:monotone}
Let $d\ge1$. Suppose $f=\sum_bw_bg_b$ is a nonnegative local conic combination of nonnegative submodular functions of arity at most $d$, and the full function $f$ is monotone. The individual $g_b$ need not be monotone. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:monotone_recovery}
 F(x)\ge\gamma_d L(x)\ge\gamma_d f^+(x).
\end{equation}
The constant is sharp. A $\delta$-accurate maximizer of $L$ over any compact feasible region gives value at least $\gamma_d(\max F-\delta)$ without coordinate decrease; down-closedness is unnecessary for this fractional conclusion.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Absorb empty-support terms into a constant. For $i\in N_b$, put
\[
 m_{b,i}=g_b(N_b)-g_b(N_b\setminus\{i\}),\qquad
 h_b(S)=g_b(S)-g_b(\varnothing)-\sum_{i\in S}m_{b,i}.
\]
Diminishing returns implies that every marginal of $h_b$ is nonnegative. Hence $h_b$ is monotone and submodular; since $h_b(\varnothing)=0$, it is also nonnegative. Let
\[
 c=f(\varnothing),\qquad
 r_i=\sum_{b:i\in N_b}w_bm_{b,i}=f(N)-f(N\setminus\{i\})\ge0.
\]
Let $H_b$ be the multilinear extension of $h_b$. Subtracting an affine function commutes with both extension operations, giving
\[
 F(x)=c+\sum_ir_ix_i+\sum_bw_bH_b(x_{N_b}),\quad
 L(x)=c+\sum_ir_ix_i+\sum_bw_bh_b^+(x_{N_b}).
\]
For a nonnegative monotone submodular function on $q$ elements, the finite-ground-set correlation inequality gives $H_b\ge\gamma_q h_b^+$ \citep[Lemma~4.10]{ChekuriVondrakZenklusen2014}. Since $\gamma_q$ is nonincreasing and $q\le d$, summing with $c,r_i,w_b\ge0$ proves \eqref{eq:monotone_recovery}. Sharpness follows from $g(S)=\mathbf 1\{S\ne\varnothing\}$ on $d$ elements at $x_i=1/d$: the closure is one and the multilinear value is $\gamma_d$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:cardinality_closure}
The local concave closure is
\[
 g^+(x)=\bar h\left(\sum_{i\in A}x_i\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Jensen's inequality gives the upper bound. If $s=\sum_i x_i<d$ and $k=\lfloor s\rfloor$, the slab $\{z\in[0,1]^A:k\le\sum_i z_i\le k+1\}$ is the convex hull of incidence vectors of sets of sizes $k$ and $k+1$. Indeed, a vertex cannot have two fractional coordinates, since they could be perturbed in opposite directions. Nor can it have exactly one: at an integer sum bound that coordinate must be integral, and away from both sum bounds it can be perturbed alone. A convex combination of these vertices representing $x$ gives a distribution attaining $\bar h(s)$. The case $s=d$ is immediate.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:cardinality}
Set $\rho_0=\rho_1=1$ and $\rho_d=1-(1-1/d)^{d-1}$ for $d\ge2$. Every nonnegative concave-cardinality function on $d$ elements satisfies
\[
 G(x)\ge\rho_d g^+(x).
\]
Moreover, the infimum of $\max_{0\le y\le x}G(y)/g^+(x)$ over this class and positive denominators equals $\rho_d$. For any nonnegative sum of such local functions, the identity map gives factor $\min_b\rho_{|N_b|}$, regardless of overlap.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
For $d=0,1$, the extension and closure are the same affine function; a positive constant witnesses sharpness of factor one. For $d\ge2$, Appendix~\ref{app:cardinality} proves the scalar inequality and its sharpness under arbitrary downward recovery. Every component uses the identity map, so summation and Theorem~\ref{thm:common} give the optimization guarantee.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:joint_frontiers}
The values in \eqref{eq:joint_frontier} satisfy
\[
 \rho_2^{\rm joint}=\tfrac12,\qquad
 \rho_d^{\rm joint}=\tfrac8{17}\quad(3\le d\le12),\qquad
 \gamma_*\le\rho_d^{\rm joint}\le\tfrac8{17}\quad(d\ge13).
\]
The cubic upper bound holds already for positive-only NNS certificates. The quadratic and cubic bounds can also be realized asymptotically relative to the original objective optimum, not only to the roof value.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
For degree two, the rank-one clipping inequalities in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:quadratic}, followed by Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed} and nonnegative aggregation, cover the entire certificate cone, including mixed-polarity atoms. Corollary~\ref{cor:twelve} and Theorem~\ref{thm:single} give the remaining lower bounds. The following constructions prove the quadratic and cubic upper bounds.

For odd $n\ge3$, use the directed cycle
\[
 F_n(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(1-x_{i+1}),\qquad
 L_n(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\min\{x_i,1-x_{i+1}\},\quad x_{n+1}=x_1.
\]
On the cube, $L_n\le n/2$, with equality only at $\bar x=\mathbf 1/2$: equality in every minimum requires $x_i=1-x_{i+1}$, and oddness forces all coordinates to be $1/2$. On $[0,\bar x]$, each derivative $1-x_{i-1}-x_{i+1}$ is nonnegative, so the largest value is $n/4$. The roof ratio is exactly $1/2$. Multiaffinity gives the full-cube maximum $(n-1)/2$, so the ratio to that optimum is $n/[2(n-1)]\to1/2$. There is no diagonal residual, so this example also applies to the hybrid quadratic roof.

For the cubic bound, fix $0<\eta<1$ and put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic_obstruction}
 \begin{split}
 G_\eta(x_0,x_1,x_2)&=\frac5{12\eta}x_0(1-x_1)
       +\frac12x_1(1-x_2^2)+x_2(1-x_2),\\
 U_\eta&=\frac{17}{12}-\frac\eta2,\qquad
 F_{\eta,\delta}(x,z)=G_\eta(x)+(U_\eta-\delta)z,
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
where $0<\delta<U_\eta$. Optimize over
\[
 \mathcal K_\eta=\left\{(x,z)\in[0,1]^4:
 x_0\le\eta(1-z),\quad x_1\le(1-\eta)(1-z),\quad
 x_2\le\tfrac12(1-z)\right\}.
\]
Every displayed term is nonnegative and has a positive-only rooted certificate. On this set the three nonlinear roofs equal $x_0,x_1,x_2$, respectively. Because their coefficients are positive, a roof maximizer saturates the coordinate bounds. The roof is at most
$U_\eta(1-z)+(U_\eta-\delta)z$.
Its unique maximizer is $(\eta,1-\eta,1/2,0)$ with value $U_\eta$.

Below this maximizer, $z=0$; monotonicity in the first coordinate permits $x_0=\eta$. Writing $s=x_1$ and $t=x_2$, the objective becomes
\[
 \frac5{12}(1-s)+\frac12s(1-t^2)+t(1-t).
\]
For fixed $t$, it is affine in $s\in[0,1-\eta]$. At $s=0$ its maximum is $2/3$ at $t=1/2$. At $s=1-\eta$, its maximum over $0\le t\le1/2$ is
\[
 \frac12-\frac\eta{12}+\frac1{2(3-\eta)}\le\frac23.
\]
The lower-box maximum is therefore $2/3$, and its ratio to $U_\eta$ tends to $8/17$. The incomparable feasible point $(0,0,0,1)$ has value $U_\eta-\delta$, so the ratio to the true optimum has the same upper limit as $\eta,\delta\downarrow0$. This cubic example belongs to every larger nested literal-degree class.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:best_representation}
The method first maximizes \eqref{eq:best_representation_roof} over a nonempty compact down-closed set and then may return the best point in $[0,\bar x]$, where $\bar x$ is a roof maximizer. Its largest universal ratio, required to hold for every roof maximizer and measured relative to the true multilinear optimum, is $1/2$ for nonnegative submodular polynomials of degree at most two and $8/17$ for those of degree at most three.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
For a quadratic $F$, choose the degree-two representation constructed by Theorem~\ref{thm:orientation}; clipping recovers at least $L_{\mathcal R}(x)/2\ge L_F^*(x)/2$. For a cubic $F$, choose the degree-three representation constructed by Proposition~\ref{prop:cubic_certificate}; Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic_maps} gives weighted recovered value at least $8L_{\mathcal R}(x)/17\ge8L_F^*(x)/17$. Theorem~\ref{thm:common} proves the lower bounds at a maximizer of $L_F^*$. Appendix~\ref{app:representation_frontiers} expresses the remaining coefficient freedom as a linear program and constructs instances for which it cannot change the roof. Augmented odd cycles prove the quadratic upper bound; the cubic graph construction proves the cubic upper bound, with all roof maximizers agreeing on the coordinates relevant to the objective.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:aggregate_frontier}
The aggregate value is $\rho_4^{\rm agg}=8/17$. The upper bound already uses local functions of arity three and permits arbitrary joint downward recovery.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The lower bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:arity_four}. Appendix~\ref{app:overlap} constructs, for every integer $q\ge2$, an arity-three local decomposition and a point $\bar x_q$ at which
\[
 L(\bar x_q)=\frac{17}{12}-\frac1{2q},\qquad
 \max_{0\le y\le\bar x_q}F(y)=\frac23.
\]
The resulting ratio $8q/(17q-6)$ decreases to $8/17$. The point $\bar x_q$ maximizes the additive roof over its lower box.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:thirteen}
The supremum of finite common-coordinatewise downward portfolio factors satisfies
\[
 \rho_{13}^{\rm cw}<\frac8{17}.
\]
Thus $8/17$ cannot even be approached by such portfolios through literal degree thirteen, irrespective of their number of branches or the regularity of their maps.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The cubic witness in \eqref{eq:cubic_obstruction} shows that every such factor is at most $8/17$: its roof tends to $17/12$ while every downward value is at most $2/3$. Suppose that portfolios certify factors $\rho_j\to8/17$, and choose $\eta_j\downarrow0$ with $0<\eta_j<1$. For a random branch of the $j$th portfolio, write
\[
 q=\phi(1-\eta_j),\qquad t=\phi(1/2),\qquad
 (q,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,1/2],
\]
and let $\mathbb E_j$ denote expectation over its finite branch distribution. For the function $H$ defined above, replacing $\phi(\eta_j)/\eta_j$ by its upper bound one only increases the recovered value of $G_{\eta_j}$ at $(\eta_j,1-\eta_j,1/2)$. The termwise guarantee then implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:thirteen_cubic_moment}
 \mathbb E_j H(q,t)\ge\rho_j\left(\frac{17}{12}-\frac{\eta_j}{2}\right).
\end{equation}
The positive rank-one midpoint atom gives the second necessary inequality
\begin{equation}\label{eq:thirteen_pair_moment}
 \mathbb E_j[t(1-t)]\ge\frac{\rho_j}{2}.
\end{equation}
Finally, put
\[
 b=1-\left(\frac{23}{24}\right)^{12}<\frac25,
 \qquad \frac25-b=\frac{12079851931877}{182601737180282880}>0.
\]
For a complemented atom with root $a=1/2$ and twelve heads $u_i=1/24$, the roof is $1/2$. Downwardness bounds every recovered head coordinate by $1/24$, so its branch value is at most $b(1-t)$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:thirteen_head_moment}
 b\mathbb E_j(1-t)\ge\frac{\rho_j}{2}.
\end{equation}

The three moments in \eqref{eq:thirteen_cubic_moment}--\eqref{eq:thirteen_head_moment} belong to the convex hull of the continuous image
\[
 (q,t)\longmapsto\bigl(H(q,t),\ t(1-t),\ 1-t\bigr)
\]
of the compact rectangle $[0,1]\times[0,1/2]$. This convex hull is compact in $\mathbb R^3$: by Carath\'eodory's theorem, each of its points is a convex combination of at most four image points. A convergent subsequence therefore yields a limiting moment vector represented by a finite probability distribution on the rectangle.

The identity \eqref{eq:thirteen_deficit_identity} bounds $H$ by $2/3$ and identifies its two equality points. Equation~\eqref{eq:thirteen_cubic_moment} forces the limiting expectation to equal $2/3$, so its representing distribution is supported on these two points. Let $w$ be its mass on $(1,1/3)$. The limit of \eqref{eq:thirteen_pair_moment} gives
\[
 \frac{1-w}{4}+\frac{2w}{9}\ge\frac4{17},
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad w\le\frac9{17}.
\]
The limiting left side of \eqref{eq:thirteen_head_moment} is then at most
\[
 b\left(\frac{1-w}{2}+\frac{2w}{3}\right)
 \le\frac{10b}{17}<\frac4{17},
\]
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:grouping}
Every $L_\Pi$ is concave and Boolean-exact, and
\[
 F\le f^+\le L_{\Pi'}\le L_\Pi\le L
 \qquad\text{whenever }\Pi\preceq\Pi'.
\]
The singleton partition gives $L$, and the one-block partition gives $f^+$. Any common recovery inequality paying $\rho L$ also pays $\rho L_\Pi$ and retains its guarantee after optimizing $L_\Pi$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Mixing feasible fixed-marginal distributions proves concavity, and Boolean marginals force a point mass. Projecting a global distribution onto the block ground sets gives $f^+\le L_\Pi$. When two blocks merge, each expected contribution under a joint distribution is bounded by its separate closure. Maximizing the joint expectation therefore shows that merging cannot increase the roof. The endpoint identities follow from the definitions. Finally, $L_\Pi\le L$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:common} give the recovery guarantee.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:junction}
Given a width-$\tau_C$ tree decomposition $T_C$ of the interaction graph of block $C$, its exact closure has a linear formulation with $O(|T_C|2^{\tau_C+1})$ bag-probability variables and separator-consistency constraints. Thus fixed supplied widths yield polynomial-size grouped roof formulations.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Each local ground set is a clique, so it lies in some bag. Assign its objective to one such bag. For each bag, introduce a joint probability table, normalize it, prescribe its singleton marginals, and require adjacent bags to agree on their full intersection tables. The running-intersection property lets us glue these distributions successively into a global law. Conditional laws on zero-probability separator states can be chosen arbitrarily, since they carry no mass. Conversely, every global law induces consistent bag tables. The formulation is therefore exact, and counting table entries gives the size bound \citep{WainwrightJordan2008}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite_game}
For a finite nonempty row set $J$ and $k\ge1$ candidate maps,
\[
 \max_{p\in\Delta([k])}\min_{r\in J}(Ap)_r
 =\min_{w\in\Delta(J)}\max_{s\in[k]}(A^\top w)_s.
\]
For common-coordinatewise maps, the dual mixture is realizable on disjoint copies of the rows: weighting row $r$ by $w_r/u_r$ gives total additive roof one and branch values $(A^\top w)_s$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The equality is finite linear-programming duality. Independent copies have additive roofs and objectives, and the prescribed weights normalize their roof contributions.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:dual_cone}
Fix $\rho\ge0$ and a finite portfolio $\{(p_s,R_s)\}$, where $R_s$ maps $[0,1]^A$ into itself. The portfolio satisfies
\[
 \sum_sp_sG_g(R_s(x))\ge\rho g^+(x)
 \quad(g\in\mathcal S_A,\ x\in[0,1]^A)
\]
if and only if, for every distribution $\mu$ on $2^A$, with marginals $x(\mu)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dual_cone}
 \sum_sp_s\nu_{R_s(x(\mu))}-\rho\mu
 \in\operatorname{cone}\{e_S,s_{ij,T}:S,i,j,T\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The finitely generated cone on the right is $\mathcal S_A^*$ by polyhedral duality. Pairing \eqref{eq:dual_cone} with any $g\in\mathcal S_A$ and maximizing over couplings with fixed marginals proves sufficiency. Conversely, the stated inequality dominates $\rho\mu^\top g$ for every such $g$, so the left vector belongs to the dual cone.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:vertex}
For every multilinear $F$,
\[
 \max_{0\le y\le x}F(y)=\max_{M\subseteq N}F(x\odot\mathbf 1_M).
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
With the other coordinates fixed, the objective is affine in each coordinate. Move that coordinate to a maximizing endpoint and repeat for all coordinates.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:retention_game}
If $J_x\ne\varnothing$, the largest guarantee supplied by one random retained-coordinate set simultaneously for all allowed local conic combinations equals
\begin{equation}\label{eq:retention_game}
 \rho^*(x)=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta(2^N)}\min_{j\in J_x}\sum_M\lambda_M A_{jM}
 =\min_{\theta\in\Delta(J_x)}\max_{M\subseteq N}\sum_j\theta_j A_{jM}.
\end{equation}
An optimal $\lambda$ satisfies $\mathbb E_M F(x\odot\mathbf 1_M)\ge\rho^*(x)L(x)$ for every allowed instance. A dual optimum is realized by assigning coefficient $\theta_j/r^+(x_E)$ to the corresponding ray on support $E$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
If one distribution pays every ray, it pays every allowed conic combination: the multilinear extension is linear, while concave closure is subadditive under nonnegative addition. Rows with zero roof value need only a nonnegative contribution, so they can be omitted. Conversely, each positive-roof ray is an allowed local function, making the minimum over rows necessary. Finite linear-programming duality gives the second expression. The stated coefficients make the dual instance's additive roof equal to one.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:anytime}
The sequence $U_k$ is nonincreasing and $V_k$ is nondecreasing. Whenever $U_k>0$, the value $V_k/U_k$ certifies the retained solution's approximation ratio relative to $\max_\mathcal K F$, and these certificates are nondecreasing. If the final partition has one block, $U_m=\max_\mathcal K f^+$, not necessarily $\max_\mathcal K F$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:grouping} makes the upper bounds decrease, while retaining earlier recovered points makes the feasible values increase. Since $\max_\mathcal K F\le U_k$, division gives the certificate.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:rounding}
Let $\rho,\eta,\delta\ge0$. Suppose recovery gives $y\in\mathcal K$ with $F(y)\ge\rho(\max_\mathcal K F-\delta)$, and a rounding procedure returns $S\in\mathcal I$ with $\mathbb E f(S)\ge\eta F(y)$. Then
\[
 \mathbb E f(S)\ge\eta\rho\left(\max_{T\in\mathcal I}f(T)-\delta\right).
\]
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Every $\mathbf 1_T$, $T\in\mathcal I$, belongs to $\mathcal K$, so $\max_\mathcal K F\ge\max_{T\in\mathcal I}f(T)$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:discrete}
Under no side constraint, an at-most-$k$ constraint, or a matroid-independence constraint, the following fractional factors transfer without further loss, subject to the representation and access assumptions already stated: $1/2$ for $\mathcal Q_2$; $8/17$ for $\mathcal Q_3$, supplied $\mathcal R_{12}$ representations, and supplied $\mathcal C_4$ decompositions; $\gamma_*$ for supplied arbitrary-finite-arity $\mathcal R_\infty$ representations; and $\min_b\rho_{|N_b|}$ for supplied concave-cardinality decompositions. Globally monotone members of $\mathcal C_d$ have factor $\gamma_d$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:rounding} with $\eta=1$ to the corresponding roof-recovery results.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:correlation}
For every $x$,
\[
 F(x)\le\max_{0\le y\le x}F(y)\le\mathbb E f_{\max}(R_x).
\]
Consequently $\operatorname{CG}(f)\le\operatorname{DCG}(f)\le\operatorname{CG}_{\max}(f)$. A downward recovery inequality paying $\rho L(x)$ with $L\ge f^+$ implies $\operatorname{DCG}(f),\operatorname{CG}_{\max}(f)\ge\rho$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
For $y\le x$, sample $R_x$ and retain element $i$ independently with probability $y_i/x_i$, using zero when $x_i=0$. The retained set has law $R_y$ and is contained in $R_x$, so $F(y)\le\mathbb E f_{\max}(R_x)$. Maximizing and then taking infima proves the claims.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:online_monotone}
If $f\in\mathcal C_d$ is globally monotone, $x$ is a $\delta$-accurate maximizer of its local roof over $P_{\mathcal I}$, and a $(b,c)$-selectable greedy OCRS is available, then its output on $R_{bx}$ satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E f(S_{\rm out})\ge bc\gamma_d\left(\max_{S\in\mathcal I}f(S)-\delta\right).
\]
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The monotone OCRS theorem gives $\mathbb E f(S_{\rm out})\ge cF(bx)$ \citep{FeldmanSvenssonZenklusen2021}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone}, followed by concavity and nonnegativity at zero of $L$, to obtain $F(bx)\ge\gamma_dL(bx)\ge b\gamma_dL(x)$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:online_preservation}
Suppose $f$ has the representation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:online_class}
 f(S)=a+\sum_ip_i\mathbf 1\{i\in S\}+\sum_iq_i\mathbf 1\{i\notin S\}
       +\sum_r\mu_r\operatorname{cov}_{E_r}(S)+\sum_r\nu_r\operatorname{cut}_{E_r,H_r}(S),
\end{equation}
with all coefficients nonnegative. A $c$-selectable randomized greedy OCRS applied to $R_z$ satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E f(S_{\rm out})\ge cF(z)
\]
for every arrival order, including one selected by an almighty adversary. In particular, the statement holds for every function in $\mathcal R_\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Consider one cut function and order $E=(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$. The disjoint events
\[
 C_k=\{e_k\in R_z,\ e_1,\ldots,e_{k-1}\notin R_z,\ H\nsubseteq R_z\}
\]
partition the event that the cut is one. Terms with $z_{e_k}=0$ have zero probability and may be omitted. Conditional on $e_k$ being active, its remaining condition is
$C_k'=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{k-1}\notin R_z,\ H\setminus\{e_k\}\nsubseteq R_z\}$.
Conditional on $\mathcal F_z$, both $C_k'$ and $Q_{e_k}$ decrease as the remaining independent activations grow, so Harris's inequality gives positive association \citep{Harris1960}. The event $C_k'$ is independent of $\mathcal F_z$, and $Q_{e_k}$ is independent of the activation of $e_k$. Averaging therefore gives
\[
 \Pr(C_k\cap Q_{e_k})\ge\Pr(C_k)\Pr(Q_{e_k})\ge c\Pr(C_k).
\]
On $C_k\cap Q_{e_k}$, the algorithm accepts an element of $E$, while an inactive element of $H$ remains absent. The output cut is therefore one. Summing proves preservation of its expectation. Omitting the missing-$H$ condition gives the coverage result. Positive literals are preserved with probability at least $cz_i$; complemented literals satisfy $\Pr(i\notin S_{\rm out})\ge1-z_i\ge c(1-z_i)$, and constants lose no value. Sum these bounds with the nonnegative coefficients.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{hard:prop:equal-marginal}
If random variables $X,Y$ have identical distributions and $g$ is Boolean,
then
\[
 \mathbb P[g(X)=1,g(Y)=0]
 =\mathbb P[g(X)=0,g(Y)=1]
 =\tfrac12\mathbb P[g(X)\ne g(Y)].
\]
For a one-type test using the same cloud function and bias at both ends,
symmetrization multiplies both completeness and soundness by two. The
soundness-to-completeness ratio is therefore unchanged whenever completeness is positive.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Since $\mathbb E[g(X)]=\mathbb E[g(Y)]$, subtracting the two crossing probabilities gives zero.
Their sum is the disagreement probability.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{hard:prop:flow}
Let $W_{st}\ge0$ be directed type-pair weights, let $g_s$ be a Boolean cloud
function of type $s$, and set $m_s=\mathbb E[g_s]$.  For every used pair $(s,t)$,
assume that $X$ has the prescribed type-$s$ marginal and $Y$ has the
prescribed type-$t$ marginal, so
$\mathbb E[g_s(X)]=m_s$ and $\mathbb E[g_t(Y)]=m_t$.  If
\begin{align*}
 A&=\sum_{s,t}W_{st}\mathbb E[g_s(X)(1-g_t(Y))],\\
 B&=\sum_{s,t}W_{st}\mathbb E[(1-g_s(X))g_t(Y)],
\end{align*}
then
\begin{equation}\label{hard:eq:flow}
 A-B=\sum_s(\operatorname{out}_s-\operatorname{in}_s)m_s,
 \quad
 \operatorname{out}_s:=\sum_tW_{st},\quad \operatorname{in}_s:=\sum_tW_{ts}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $A=B$ for every family of cloud functions when $W$ is
Eulerian, meaning $\operatorname{out}_s=\operatorname{in}_s$ for every type $s$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
For each ordered pair, the difference between forward and reverse acceptance
is $m_s-m_t$. Multiplying by the pair weights and collecting the coefficient
of each mean gives \eqref{hard:eq:flow}.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{hard:lem:binary-correlation}
Let $(X,Y)$ have a connected distribution on $\{0,1\}^2$, nondegenerate
Bernoulli marginals, and Pearson correlation $\rho$.  Its maximal
correlation
\[
 \sup\{\mathbb E[u(X)v(Y)]:\mathbb E u=\mathbb E v=0,\ \mathbb E u^2=\mathbb E v^2=1\}
\]
equals $|\rho|$.  After replacing $Y$ by $1-Y$, the Pearson correlation is
$-\rho$ and the maximal correlation remains $|\rho|$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
The centered subspace of $L^2(X)$ is one-dimensional, spanned by the
standardized variable $(X-\mathbb E X)/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}X}$; the same holds
for $Y$.  Every admissible $u,v$ is therefore one of these standardized
variables up to sign.  The supremum is the absolute Pearson correlation.
Complementation negates the standardized second variable.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{hard:lem:finite-type-invariance}
Fix a finite type system $(\mathcal T,W,\nu)$ whose used binary pair spaces
are connected.  For every $0<\eta<1$, there are an integer $d\ge1$ and
constant $0<\tau\le1$ with the following property.  Let
$g_s:\{0,1\}^R\to[0,1]$ have mean $m_s$ under the $q_s$-biased product
measure.  Write $\operatorname{Inf}_i^{\le d}(g_s)$ for the degree-at-most-$d$ influence of
coordinate $i$ in the corresponding biased Fourier basis.  Then either
\begin{equation}\label{hard:eq:finite-type-invariance}
 \sum_{s,t}W_{st}
 \mathbb E_{\nu_{st}^{\otimes R}}[g_s(X)(1-g_t(Y))]
 \le \Psi(m)+\eta,
\end{equation}
or some used pair $(s,t)$ and coordinate $i$ satisfy
\[
 \operatorname{Inf}_i^{\le d}(g_s)\ge\tau,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Inf}_i^{\le d}(g_t)\ge\tau.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Complement the second binary space and its output, giving maximal correlation $-\rho_{st}$. Mossel's two-function bound then gives $D_{\rho_{st}}(m_s,m_t)$, up to the prescribed error, unless a coordinate has large low-degree influence in both endpoint functions. Choose common influence parameters for the finite set of used pairs and sum with the normalized weights. Appendix~\ref{app:invariance_proof} gives the details and the precise source dependence.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{hard:lem:influence-decoding}
Fix a finite type system and $0<\eta<1$.  There is a constant $\kappa>0$,
independent of $R$ and of the size of $\mathcal U$, such that
\begin{align}
 &\mathbb E_{u\in U}\sum_{s,t}W_{st}
 \mathbb E_{\nu_{st}^{\otimes R}}
 [f_{u,s}(X)(1-f_{u,t}(Y))]\notag\\
 &\hspace{30mm}>
 \mathbb E_{u\in U}[\Psi(m_u)]+\eta
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{val}(\mathcal U)\ge\kappa .
 \label{hard:eq:decoding-implication}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
If acceptance exceeds the Gaussian profile on average, a positive fraction of outer vertices must have a shared influential coordinate. Convexity passes this influence from each neighbor average to a positive fraction of its incident clouds. The total low-degree influence bound limits the number of candidate labels. Choosing labels uniformly from these lists gives a positive expected fraction of satisfied edges. Appendix~\ref{app:decoding_proof} gives the constants and permutation convention.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{hard:thm:affine-criterion}
Suppose the masses, biases, type weights, and pair-distribution atoms are
rational, $C>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$, $\beta\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{hard:eq:affine-majorant}
 \Psi(z)\le\beta+\lambda\pi^\top z
 \qquad\text{for every }z\in[0,1]^{\mathcal T}.
\end{equation}
Assume also that $S:=\beta+\lambda\mu<C$.  For every
$0<\delta<(C-S)/2$, the Unique Games Conjecture implies NP-hardness of
distinguishing normalized weighted Max-DiCut instances with an
at-most-cardinality budget and $|k/n'-\mu|\le\delta$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{hard:eq:ugc-gap}
 \operatorname{OPT}\ge C-\delta
 \qquad\text{from those satisfying}\qquad
 \operatorname{OPT}\le\beta+\lambda\mu+\delta.
\end{equation}
Here $n'$ is the number of vertices and the total arc weight is normalized to
one.  Consequently, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is no polynomial-time
$((\beta+\lambda\mu)/C+\varepsilon)$-approximation on this family.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The regular long-code construction gives dictator density $\mu$ and completeness approaching $C$. Influence decoding bounds each no-case cut by the average Gaussian profile; the affine inequality bounds that average through the cardinality budget. Rational replication converts vertex masses to ordinary cardinalities. A cut may separate copies of the same vertex, but the resulting fractional cloud indicators obey the same bilinear soundness bound. Appendix~\ref{app:affine_reduction_proof} gives the construction and accounts for replication, loop removal, and the error terms.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{hard:prop:affine-dual}
For every continuous $\Psi$ and $0<\mu<1$,
\begin{align}
 S_\Psi(\mu)
 &=\min_{\lambda\ge0}
 \left\{
  \lambda\mu+
  \max_{z\in[0,1]^{\mathcal T}}
   [\Psi(z)-\lambda\pi^\top z]
 \right\}\label{hard:eq:dual-one}\\
 &=\min_{\lambda\ge0,\,\beta}
 \left\{
  \beta+\lambda\mu:
  \Psi(z)\le\beta+\lambda\pi^\top z
  \ \forall z
 \right\}.\label{hard:eq:dual-two}
\end{align}
Thus the optimal affine certificate gives the exact value
$S_\Psi(\mu)$ of the one-budget profile-mixing problem.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Lagrangian relaxation of the moment constraint gives the right-hand side of
\eqref{hard:eq:dual-one} as an upper bound.  For the reverse inequality, define
\[
 G(t):=\sup_\xi
 \left\{\int\Psi\,d\xi:\int\pi^\top z\,d\xi\le t\right\}.
\]
Compactness and continuity ensure that the supremum is attained. Mixing
feasible measures makes $G$ concave; increasing the budget makes it
nondecreasing.
At the interior point $\mu$, choose a supporting supergradient
$\lambda\ge0$.  A point mass at $z$ is feasible for budget $\pi^\top z$, so
\[
 \Psi(z)-\lambda\pi^\top z
 \le G(\mu)-\lambda\mu.
\]
Taking the maximum over $z$ gives the reverse inequality.  Introducing
$\beta=\max_z[\Psi(z)-\lambda\pi^\top z]$ gives
\eqref{hard:eq:dual-two}.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{hard:thm:np-hardness}
For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, it is NP-hard to approximate
\eqref{hard:eq:qsub-cardinality} within $12/13+\varepsilon$.  The statement holds even
for weighted Max-DiCut objectives with nonnegative arc weights, no terminals,
and budget $k=n'/2$, where $n'$ is the enlarged ground-set size.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
For a weighted directed graph $D=([n],A)$, its directed-cut objective is
\[
 f_D(S)=\sum_{(i,j)\in A}w_{ij}\mathbf 1\{i\in S,\ j\notin S\}.
\]
This is an explicit quadratic submodular pseudo-Boolean function that is
nonnegative on the whole cube.  Trevisan et al.\ prove that it is NP-hard to
approximate unconstrained Max-DiCut within $12/13+\varepsilon$
\citep{TrevisanSorkinSudanWilliamson2000}.

Add $n$ isolated vertices and set $k=n$ on the resulting $n'=2n$ vertices.
Every original cut now satisfies the budget. Conversely, removing selected
isolated vertices preserves its value. The two optima are equal, so an
approximation for the constrained instance gives the same factor for the
original instance.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{hard:prop:gaussian-certificate}
For every $(a,b)\in[0,1]^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{hard:eq:certified-affine}
 \Psi(a,b)\le
 \frac{58213}{1000000}
 +\frac{64713}{100000}
 \left(\frac{a}{1000000}+\frac{999999b}{1000000}\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{hard:app:certificate} bounds the quadrature error and derives
coordinatewise nonincreasing derivative bounds. The verifier combines these
bounds with 256-bit MPFR evaluation and explicit outward allowances.
Adaptive subdivision then certifies the inequality on every cell.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{hard:thm:ugc-hardness}
Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is no
polynomial-time
\[
 \left(
  \frac{118590464878885}{143151448765848}+\varepsilon
 \right)
 =\left(0.828426578293753\ldots+\varepsilon\right)
\]
approximation for \eqref{hard:eq:qsub-cardinality}.  The hardness holds for the
terminal-free Max-DiCut subclass at asymptotic budget density
\[
 \frac{k}{n'}=\frac{186600729}{2000000000}+o(1)
 =0.0933003645+o(1).
\]
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Use Theorem~\ref{hard:thm:affine-criterion} with
\[
 \beta=\frac{58213}{1000000},
 \qquad
 \lambda=\frac{64713}{100000}.
\]
Proposition~\ref{hard:prop:gaussian-certificate} bounds soundness. Dividing
this bound by completeness gives
\[
 \frac{\beta+\lambda\mu}{C}
 =\frac{118590464878885}{143151448765848}
 =0.828426578293753\ldots.
\]
The reduction directly produces a directed-cut objective with nonnegative
arc weights, hence an explicit instance of \eqref{hard:eq:qsub-cardinality}.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:quasirandom}
For all sufficiently large integers $m$, there are triangle-free graphs $G_m=(V_m,E_m)$, $|V_m|=m$, such that, with $Z_m=2|E_m|$, uniformly over $A\subseteq V_m$ and $u=|A|/m$,
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{vol}_{G_m}(A)}{Z_m}=u+o(1),\qquad
 \frac{e_{G_m}(A)}{Z_m}=\frac{u^2}{2}+o(1).
\]
Here $e_G(A)$ counts edges internal to $A$, and $\operatorname{vol}_G(A)$ is the sum of degrees in $A$. Uniform $o(1)$ means that the maximum absolute error over all subsets $A$ tends to zero as $m\to\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Start with the random graph $G(m,p)$, in which each pair of the $m$ vertices is independently an edge with probability $p=m^{-2/3}$. For any fixed $A$, the induced-edge count is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables with variance at most $pm^2/2$. The exponential bound
\[
 \Pr(|X-\mathbb E X|\ge t)\le2\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(\operatorname{Var}X+t/3)}\right)
\]
follows from the exponential-moment bound for Bernoulli sums. Taking $t=Cm^{7/6}$ with a sufficiently large constant and a union bound over $2^m$ sets yields, with probability tending to one,
\[
 e(A)=p\binom{|A|}{2}+O(m^{7/6})
       =p\binom{|A|}{2}+o(pm^2)
\]
uniformly. The expected number of triangles is $O(m)$, so Markov's inequality makes it at most $m\log m$ with probability tending to one. Choose a realization satisfying both events, then delete one edge from each triangle. At most $m\log m=o(pm^2)$ edges are deleted, preserving the uniform estimate and $|E_m|=(1+o(1))pm^2/2$. Finally,
\[
 \operatorname{vol}_{G_m}(A)=|E_m|+e_{G_m}(A)-e_{G_m}(V_m\setminus A)
\]
gives the volume estimate after division by $Z_m$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:certificate_separation}
The polynomial $G$ in \eqref{eq:map_counterexample_C} does not admit a nonnegative compatible continuous rooted certificate of literal degree at most twelve.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Such a certificate would induce a concave Boolean-exact roof $L\ge g^+$ by the minimality of concave closure. Theorem~\ref{thm:twelve_atoms} and Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed} would then give
$8G(\alpha_{12}(x))+9G(\beta_{12}(x))\ge8L(x)\ge8g^+(x)$,
contradicting \eqref{eq:map_counterexample_C}.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:outcome_transfer}
Assume the valuation on all of $U$ has representation \eqref{eq:online_class}. For $z\in bP^{\rm out}$ and an item-space $(b,c)$-selectable greedy OCRS, activate realized outcome $e$ independently with probability $z_e/p_e$, interpreted as zero when $p_e=0$, and run the OCRS on the corresponding item. The resulting feasible outcome set satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E f(S_{\rm alg})\ge cF(z).
\]
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Put $\bar z_i=\sum_{e\in U_i}z_e$. Item activations are independent with marginals $\bar z\in bP_{\mathcal I}$. An equivalent procedure independently chooses a candidate outcome for each item with $\bar z_i>0$, using probabilities $z_e/\bar z_i$, and then activates the candidate with probability $\bar z_i$. Conditional on these candidates, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:online_preservation}. Restricting to the candidate set preserves \eqref{eq:online_class}: a cut becomes a cut, a coverage indicator, or zero, and unaries may become constants. Because the OCRS depends only on $\bar z$ and is independent of the candidate identities, its selectability remains $c$ for every fixed candidate set.

Let $A_z$ be the set of activated candidates, which contains at most one
outcome per item. Averaging the conditional OCRS inequalities gives
$\mathbb E f(S_{\rm alg})\ge c\mathbb E f(A_z)$. It remains to show $\mathbb E f(A_z)\ge F(z)$.
Conditional on the other items, the submodular function $h$ on one item's outcomes satisfies
\[
 h(S)\le h(\varnothing)+\sum_{e\in S}\bigl(h(\{e\})-h(\varnothing)\bigr).
\]
Taking an independent sample with marginals $(z_e)_{e\in U_i}$ bounds its expectation by
$(1-\bar z_i)h(\varnothing)+\sum_e z_eh(\{e\})$,
which is the expectation for that item under $A_z$. Replace the item blocks one
at a time to prove this comparison. This is the
submodular-dominance mechanism relevant here \citep{QiuSingla2022}.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:prophet_interface}
Under Proposition~\ref{prop:outcome_transfer}, assume the item-space OCRS is efficient and let $\alpha,\varepsilon\ge0$. Any efficiently computed $z\in bP^{\rm out}$ satisfying $F(z)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm prop}-\varepsilon$ gives an online guarantee
\[
 \mathbb E f(S_{\rm alg})\ge c\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm prop}-c\varepsilon.
\]
In particular, suppose the full outcome valuation also has an efficiently optimizable roof and a downward recovery inequality of factor $\rho$. Then a $\delta$-accurate roof optimizer gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:roof_prophet}
 \mathbb E f(S_{\rm alg})\ge bc\rho(\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm prop}-\delta).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
The first assertion is Proposition~\ref{prop:outcome_transfer}. For the second, optimize $L$ over \eqref{eq:outcome_polytope}, recover $y\le x$ with $F(y)\ge\rho L(x)$, and set $z=by$. Then $z\in bP^{\rm out}$. Since $y\ge0$ and every entry of $\nabla^2F$ is nonpositive, $d^2F(ty)/dt^2=y^\top\nabla^2F(ty)y\le0$. Concavity and $F(0)\ge0$ give $F(by)\ge bF(y)$. Apply \eqref{eq:prophet_roof_bound}.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
For a used pair $(s,t)$, put $Y':=1-Y$ and
$h_t(y'):=1-g_t(1-y')$.  Apply Mossel's two-function theorem to $g_s$ and
$h_t$ on the correlated space $(X,Y')$.  By
Lemma~\ref{hard:lem:binary-correlation}, its maximal correlation is $-\rho_{st}$, so
the Gaussian upper bound is
\[
 \Gamma_{-\rho_{st}}(m_s,1-m_t)
 =D_{\rho_{st}}(m_s,m_t).
\]
The two-function refinement applies whenever no coordinate has large
low-degree influence in both functions \citep[Theorem~6.3 and Lemma~6.8, arXiv:math/0703683v6]{Mossel2010}; input and output
complementation do not change influence.  Choose the same $d,\tau$ for the finitely many used pairs and apply each
pairwise bound with error $\eta$. Multiplying by
$W_{st}$ and using $\sum_{s,t}W_{st}=1$ proves
\eqref{hard:eq:finite-type-invariance}.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{hard:lem:finite-type-invariance} with error $\eta/2$, obtaining
$d$ and $\tau$.  Let $B\subseteq U$ be the vertices where the family $(f_{u,s})_s$
satisfies the influence alternative.  Outside $B$, the
local test value is at most $\Psi(m_u)+\eta/2$; on $B$, its excess over
$\Psi(m_u)$ is at most one.  Thus \eqref{hard:eq:decoding-implication} implies
$|B|/|U|>\eta/2$.

For every $u\in B$, fix a witness $(s_u,t_u,i_u)$.  The first endpoint function
has influence at least $\tau$, so label $u$ by $i_u$.
Convexity of squared biased Fourier coefficients gives
\[
 \operatorname{Inf}_{i_u}^{\le d}(f_{u,s_u})
 \le \mathbb E_{v\in N(u)}
 \operatorname{Inf}_{\sigma_{uv}(i_u)}^{\le d}(g_{v,s_u}).
\]
Consequently, for at least a $\tau/2$ fraction of the incident edges,
$\operatorname{Inf}_{\sigma_{uv}(i_u)}^{\le d}(g_{v,s_u})\ge\tau/2$.  For $v\in V$, set
\[
 I_v:=\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal T}
 \{j:\operatorname{Inf}_j^{\le d}(g_{v,s})\ge\tau/2\}.
\]
The total low-degree influence bound gives
$|I_v|\le M:=\lceil2|\mathcal T|d/\tau\rceil$.  Label each $v$ uniformly
from $I_v$, using an arbitrary label when $I_v$ is empty.  For each qualifying edge $(u,v)$, the label $\sigma_{uv}(i_u)$ belongs to $I_v$
and is chosen with probability at least $1/M$. Under our permutation
convention, this choice satisfies the edge. Regularity and the fraction of
qualifying incident edges give an expected satisfied-edge fraction of at least
\[
 \frac{|B|}{|U|}\frac{\tau}{2M}
 >\frac{\eta\tau}{4M}=:\kappa.
\]
Some deterministic labeling attains this value.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Use the regular long-code construction with a global cardinality constraint
\citep{RaghavendraTan2012,AustrinStankovic2019}.  For every $v\in V$ and
$s\in\mathcal T$, create a type-$s$ cloud indexed by $x\in\{0,1\}^R$ with
vertex mass
\[
 \frac1{|V|}\pi_s\mathbb P_{q_s}[x].
\]
Sample an arc by choosing $u\in U$ uniformly and ordered neighbors
$v,w\in N(u)$ independently. Choose $(s,t)$ with probability $W_{st}$,
draw $(X,Y)\sim\nu_{st}^{\otimes R}$, and apply the edge permutations.
Place the arc from the type-$s$ cloud of $v$ to the type-$t$ cloud of $w$.  For a cut with cloud indicators $g_{v,s}$, its value
is exactly the left-hand side of \eqref{hard:eq:decoding-implication}, with
$f_{u,s}$ as in \eqref{hard:eq:neighbor-average}.

Suppose a labeling satisfies at least $1-\zeta$ of the Unique-Games edges.
Select in each cloud the dictator coordinate given by its right-vertex label.
The selected vertex mass is exactly $\mu$.  Both sampled constraints are
satisfied with probability at least $1-2\zeta$; conditional on this event the
two pulled-back dictators use the same coordinate and a type-$(s,t)$ arc is
cut with probability $\nu_{st}(1,0)$.  Nonnegativity of arc weights gives
completeness at least $(1-2\zeta)C$.

For soundness, fix $\eta>0$ and take $\kappa$ from
Lemma~\ref{hard:lem:influence-decoding}. Invoke the Unique Games Conjecture with no-case value at most $\kappa/2$, so that the decoding contrapositive applies.
Equation~\eqref{hard:eq:decoding-implication} then bounds every cut by
$\mathbb E_u[\Psi(m_u)]+\eta$. Regularity expresses its selected vertex mass as
$\mathbb E_u[\pi^\top m_u]$.  A budget density at most $\mu+r$ and
\eqref{hard:eq:affine-majorant} therefore give
\[
 \text{cut value}
 \le\beta+\lambda(\mu+r)+\eta.
\]

Because all cloud probabilities are fixed rationals, replace a cloud vertex
of rational mass by the corresponding number of equal-mass copies.  Replace
each original arc by the complete bipartite bundle between its two copy sets,
distributing the arc weight by the product of the endpoint copy proportions.
For an arbitrary cut of the replicated instance, define $g_{v,s}(x)\in[0,1]$
as the selected fraction of the copies of $(v,s,x)$.  By bilinearity, its cut value and selected-vertex fraction are given by the
same expressions with these fractional indicators. Soundness therefore holds
even for cuts that separate copies. For a fixed gap tolerance, the denominators
of the type masses and product probabilities, the alphabet size $R$, and the
additional replication factor are constants. Both the number $n'$ of copies
and the explicit rational arc list are consequently polynomial in the outer
instance size. Multiplying all copy counts by a further integer $M$ makes
every copy set have at least $M$ vertices. In a bundle from a cloud vertex to itself, self-loops carry at most a $1/M$
fraction of the bundle weight. They contribute zero to every cut, so delete
them and normalize the remaining arc weight to one.
If their total weight is $\ell\le1/M$, the soundness bound is divided by
$1-\ell$, while completeness cannot decrease. Taking
$k=\lceil\mu n'\rceil$ gives $k/n'=\mu+o(1)$.
Choose $\zeta$, $\eta$, $1/M$, and the resulting density error $r$
sufficiently small relative to $\delta$.  The Unique Games Conjecture then yields the gap
\eqref{hard:eq:ugc-gap}.  If an approximation ratio exceeded $(\beta+\lambda\mu)/C$ by a fixed
amount, choosing $\delta$ sufficiently small would make the algorithm's
output values distinguish the two cases.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
